title: Senior's toolkit: numbers you can trust
summary: The settings, types and debugger windows experienced developers use so numbers do not silently break.

steps.title: Senior's toolkit: numbers you can trust
steps.body: Wrong numbers rarely crash. They overflow, round or drift quietly, and someone in finance finds them a month later. These are the tools experienced developers use to catch that early.

toolkit.what: Make integer overflow throw `OverflowException` instead of silently wrapping around to a negative number.
flags: check every operation in a block
allow wrapping on purpose, for example in a hash function
toolkit.when: money, counters and sizes, where a wrapped value would be a silent bug

toolkit.what: A project setting that makes all integer arithmetic checked by default. Some teams turn it on in Debug builds to catch overflows while testing.
flags: every `+ - * /` on integers is checked unless wrapped in `unchecked`
only in Debug builds, so Release keeps full speed

toolkit.what: Use `decimal` for money. It stores base-10 digits exactly, so `0.1m + 0.2m` is exactly `0.3m`. `double` is for measurements, where tiny errors do not matter.
flags: the suffix that makes a literal a `decimal`
use instead of `int` for counts that can pass 2,147,483,647

toolkit.what: Round on purpose. The default is banker's rounding (`2.5` becomes `2`), which surprises people who expect school rounding.
flags: the number of decimal places to keep
2.5 -> 3, the way most people and invoices expect

toolkit.what: Format numbers for people with a format string, instead of building text by hand.
At a breakpoint, Locals shows every variable in scope and Watch shows any expression you type, such as `price * quantity`, with its exact value.
flags: every local variable, updated at each step
expressions you choose; they stay between runs
point at a variable in the editor to see its value
toolkit.example: F9 on the line, F5 to run, add `price * quantity` to Watch
toolkit.when: a number is wrong and you want to see where it goes wrong

steps.prompt: Match each format string to what it prints for its value.
Arithmetic is unchecked by default. What does this print?
steps.explain: Adding 1 to the largest `int` wraps around to the smallest one, silently. `checked` (or the project setting) turns this into an `OverflowException`; `long` gives room to grow.
The default rounding sends a midpoint to the even neighbour. And `0.1 + 0.2` in `double` is `0.30000000000000004`, so it is not equal to `0.3`.

steps.prompt: A support ticket: "The page-view counter for our biggest customer suddenly shows **-2,147,483,104**." What happened, and what is the fix?
options: The `int` counter passed 2,147,483,647 and wrapped around; store it as `long` and use `checked` so the next overflow throws instead of lying
Someone subtracted views by mistake; add an `if (views < 0)` check before saving
The database is corrupt; restore the backup
`int` cannot hold large numbers on 64-bit machines; recompile for 32-bit
steps.explain: A huge negative number that is close to `int.MinValue` is the fingerprint of overflow. Widen the type, and make overflow loud with `checked` so it can never be silent again.

items: A tax rate applied to a price
The distance between two GPS points
Bytes uploaded by all users this year

steps.title: Make it a habit
steps.body: Any time a number means money, use `decimal` and round once, on purpose, with the rounding rule written down. Any time a counter could grow for years, use `long` or `checked`. When a number looks wrong, stop at a breakpoint and read it in Locals instead of guessing.
